summary: Multi-dimensional web research on Agentic Coding/Engineering ROI, governance, security, market trends for a C-Level banking pitch (Raiffeisen Schweiz)

findings.dimension: ROI & Productivity — does agentic coding actually make developers more productive, and by how much?

key_findings.claim: The most rigorous evidence (RCT, gold standard) found AI made experienced developers SLOWER, not faster — the opposite of perception. This is the single most important counter-narrative for a C-level audience to hear.
key_findings.evidence: METR's randomized controlled trial: 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 real tasks on mature repos (avg 22k+ GitHub stars, 1M+ lines). Developers took 19% LONGER with AI (Cursor Pro + Claude 3.5/3.7). They forecast a 24% speedup and, even AFTER the slowdown, still believed AI had sped them up 20% — a ~39-point perception-vs-reality gap.

key_findings.claim: METR's own 2026 follow-up did NOT cleanly reverse to a speedup — secondary outlets misreport a '+18%'. METR found the original cohort at -18% and new recruits at -4%, both with confidence intervals crossing zero, and concluded selection bias makes the data 'only very weak evidence.' Honest read: still no robust proof of speedup for experienced devs on mature code.
key_findings.evidence: Original developers: -18% speedup (CI -38% to +9%); newly-recruited: -4% (CI -15% to +9%). 30-50% of developers reported avoiding tasks they wouldn't want to do without AI, systematically removing high-impact use cases. METR scrapped task-level randomization and is redesigning the experiment.

key_findings.claim: The largest independent telemetry study (NOT a survey, NOT vendor-marketing of a coding tool) confirms a real throughput gain but a simultaneous, large quality/stability penalty — the 'Acceleration Whiplash'. This is the most decision-relevant single source for a bank.
key_findings.evidence: Faros AI, 22,000 developers / 4,000+ teams / 2 years of pipeline telemetry: task throughput per dev +33.7%, epics per dev +66%, PR merge rate +16.2%, acceptance of AI code 20%→60%. BUT: bugs per developer +54%, code churn ~10x, incidents-per-PR ~3x (+242.7%), monthly incidents +57.9%, PRs merged with NO review +31.3%, median review time ~5x.

key_findings.claim: Google's DORA 2025 report (independent, ~5,000 pros) flips its own prior-year negative finding: AI is now linked to HIGHER delivery throughput — but frames AI as an 'amplifier' of existing team capability, not a fix. Critically, DORA 2024 had found AI adoption REDUCED throughput and stability, so the trend is improving but recently volatile.
key_findings.evidence: 90% of dev professionals use AI (up 14 pts YoY); median 2 hrs/day on AI; 80%+ report productivity gains; 59% report positive code-quality effect; throughput now positively linked to AI (reversal of 2024). DORA 2024: every +25pp AI adoption was associated with -1.5% throughput and -7.2% stability. Trust remains low: only 24% trust AI 'a lot/great deal'.

key_findings.claim: Independent consultancy Bain calls the realized gains 'unremarkable' and explains WHY via Amdahl's Law: code-writing is only ~25-35% of the SDLC, so even a 100% coding speedup caps system-level gains at ~15-25% — and time saved often isn't redirected to value, so even modest gains don't reliably translate to ROI.
key_findings.evidence: Bain Technology Report 2025: developers report 'perhaps 10 to 15 percent' productivity improvement; writing+testing code is '~25-35% of the total development process'; 'the time saved often isn't redirected toward higher-value work, so even the modest gains... have not translated into positive returns.' Roughly six independent studies converge on a ~10% system-level ceiling.

key_findings.claim: Vendor/consultant-sponsored RCTs and case studies report large gains, but skew optimistic and measure narrow tasks (isolated coding, not end-to-end delivery). Useful as upper-bound, NOT as expected outcome.
key_findings.evidence: Microsoft/MIT/Princeton/Wharton 3-RCT study (4,867 devs at Microsoft, Accenture, a Fortune-100 mfr): +26.08% pull requests/week, larger gains for junior devs. Accenture arm: +8.7% PRs/dev, +84% successful builds. McKinsey: code-writing in ~half the time, refactoring ~one-third faster, Copilot users 56% faster on isolated tasks; but warns 'simply giving developers AI tools does not meaningfully move the needle.'

key_findings.claim: The agentic vs. autocomplete distinction is real and material: 2026 tools run autonomous multi-step loops, not next-line suggestions. This shifts where gains (and risks) come from — bigger, multi-file changes that strain review, exactly the Faros bottleneck.
key_findings.evidence: Anthropic 2026 report: AI now used in ~60% of dev work but only 0-20% of tasks fully delegable (the 'delegation gap'); session length 4 min (autocomplete) → 23 min (agentic), ~47 tool calls/session; 78% of Claude Code sessions involve multi-file edits (Q1 2026) vs 34% (Q1 2025). TELUS: 13,000+ custom AI solutions, ships code 30% faster, 500,000+ hours saved. Note: Anthropic is a vendor.

key_findings.claim: Stack Overflow's large independent developer survey shows usage rising but trust and favorability FALLING — a leading indicator that practitioners themselves see the gap between hype and reality.
key_findings.evidence: 2025 survey (~49,000 devs, 177 countries): 84% use/plan to use AI (up from 76%); but favorability fell from 70%+ (2023-24) to ~60%; more devs distrust AI accuracy (46%) than trust it (33%), only ~3% 'highly trust'; experienced devs most skeptical. Top frustration: AI 'almost right but not quite' (66%); debugging AI code more time-consuming (45%).

pro_arguments: Independent telemetry (Faros, 22,000 devs) confirms real, sizeable throughput gains: +33.7% tasks/dev, +66% epics/dev, +16.2% PR merge rate — this is not vendor marketing, it is before/after pipeline data within the same organizations.

Google DORA 2025 (~5,000 pros) reversed its own 2024 negative finding: AI adoption is now positively linked to higher delivery throughput, with 80%+ reporting productivity gains and 59% reporting better code quality — the trend line is improving as tooling matures.

Multiple vendor/consultant RCTs converge that gains are largest for junior/less-experienced developers (Microsoft RCT +26% PRs, juniors benefit most) — relevant for a several-hundred-developer org with a mix of seniority and onboarding needs.

Agentic (2026) tooling is materially different from 2024 autocomplete: autonomous multi-file, multi-step execution unlocks high-leverage tasks (large refactors, framework migrations, test-suite generation, onboarding to unfamiliar code) where the manual alternative is hours/days — the clearest documented ROI zone.

The METR slowdown applies specifically to senior developers on codebases they already know intimately (low room for AI to help); it explicitly does NOT claim AI fails to help most developers, and its 2026 follow-up trended less negative as developers learned the tools.

Where organizations re-architect the whole SDLC around AI (not just bolt on a coding assistant), McKinsey/Bain report 25-30% gains and top-quintile firms see 16-30% productivity and 31-45% quality improvements — the upside is real but conditional on process change, not tool purchase.

Onboarding and time-to-productivity gains are concrete: tasks like understanding unfamiliar codebases drop from weeks to hours — directly valuable for a bank with legacy systems and developer turnover.
contra_arguments: The single most rigorous study (METR RCT, the clinical-trial gold standard) found experienced devs were 19% SLOWER with AI — and the 2026 follow-up did NOT cleanly reverse this; both updated cohorts had confidence intervals crossing zero and METR itself calls the speedup evidence 'only very weak.' Be skeptical of any vendor citing METR as proof of speedup.

There is a large, documented perception-vs-reality gap: developers FEEL ~20% faster while measurably being slower. Self-reported productivity (the basis of most '80% report gains' headlines, including DORA and Stack Overflow) is therefore unreliable for a C-level investment case.

The same independent telemetry that shows throughput gains (Faros) shows the gains are partly cannibalized by quality damage: +54% bugs/dev, ~3x production incidents per PR, ~10x code churn, +31% PRs merged with NO review, ~5x review time — for a regulated bank these are direct operational-risk and audit exposures.

Amdahl's Law ceiling: code-writing is only 25-35% of the SDLC, so system-level gains are capped at ~15-25% even with perfect coding automation; ~6 independent studies converge on a real-world ceiling near ~10%. The bottleneck simply moves downstream to code review, requirements, and deployment.

Bain (independent) calls the realized savings 'unremarkable' (~10-15%) and notes the time saved is frequently NOT redirected to higher-value work, so even modest gains often fail to translate into positive ROI; ~half of GenAI-investing orgs cannot confidently calculate ROI at all.

Practitioner sentiment is cooling, not heating: Stack Overflow favorability fell from ~70% to ~60% and trust in AI accuracy dropped, with experienced devs most skeptical — a leading indicator that the early-hype gains are being reality-checked.

Cost is non-trivial and hard to forecast: agentic workloads consume 5-20x more tokens than autocomplete, landing at ~$150-250/dev/month (Anthropic's own data) before optimization — multiplied across several hundred developers this is a material, metered, usage-variable line item, not a flat seat fee.

AI-generated code volume is projected to outstrip human review capacity (~40% gap), meaning the throughput gain mechanically creates a review/quality debt unless review capacity and tooling scale in lockstep — a governance prerequisite, not an automatic benefit.
findings.confidence_notes: STRONGEST evidence: METR RCT (Jul 2025) is methodologically the cleanest but narrow (16 senior devs, mature OSS repos, early-2025 models) — do not over-generalize to a whole enterprise. Faros 2026 (22,000 devs, 2 yrs telemetry) is the best independent enterprise-scale source and the load-bearing exhibit for both the gains AND the quality tradeoff; Faros sells engineering-intelligence software (not a coding assistant), so it is not marketing the tools it measures, but it has an interest in 'measure your engineering' messaging. CAUTION on the '+18% METR reversal' circulating in blogs — that is a misread; METR's actual updated numbers still straddle zero and they explicitly downgrade the evidence due to selection bias (devs dropped out, pay was cut $150→$50/hr). VENDOR-BIASED / treat as upper bound: Anthropic 2026 report (sells Claude Code), McKinsey/Gartner (sell advisory), the Microsoft/Accenture RCT (2024, co-authored by the vendor AND pre-agentic autocomplete-era Copilot — dated for a 2026 decision). DORA 2025 is independent and credible but relies heavily on self-report, which the METR perception-gap finding shows is unreliable. The macro '~10% ceiling / Amdahl' synthesis comes from a credible secondary blog aggregating ~6 studies plus Bain — Bain itself (independent) is the strongest single anchor for the skeptical case. Key data GAP: no large, independent, agentic-era (2026) RCT yet exists — METR is rebuilding theirs; until then, the rigorous causal evidence is still based on 2025 autocomplete/early-agent tooling, while the optimistic enterprise numbers are observational/self-reported. For a FINMA-regulated bank, weight the stability/quality telemetry (incidents, unreviewed code) as heavily as the throughput numbers.

verdict.dimension: ROI & Productivity — does agentic coding actually make developers more productive, and by how much?
overturned_claims: CLAIM 5 (Bain 'unremarkable' + Amdahl's Law) — MISATTRIBUTED. The word 'unremarkable' does NOT appear in the cited Register article; Bain's own word is 'modest.' More importantly, the Amdahl's-Law framing and the '~10% system-level ceiling from six independent studies' are NOT from Bain at all — they come from an independent blogger (Philipp Dubach, philippdubach.com). By that blogger's OWN admission the 'six independent research efforts' claim is 'rhetorical rather than rigorously enumerated,' and the blog actually invokes Goldratt's Theory of Constraints, not strictly Amdahl's Law. The Register/Bain source DOES support the 10-15% gain and the 25-35%-of-SDLC figure, so the core conclusion survives — but the headline attribution ('Bain calls it unremarkable... explains via Amdahl's Law... six studies converge') is a synthesis presented as a Bain fact and must be relabeled as analyst commentary, not a hard finding.

CLAIM 2 framing ('still no robust proof of speedup' / 'did NOT cleanly reverse') — TENDENTIOUS. The numbers are accurate (orig cohort -18% CI -38%/+9%; new recruits -4% CI -15%/+9%; 30-50% task-avoidance) but the orchestrator omits METR's OWN lean: METR explicitly states it 'believes it is likely that developers are more sped up from AI in early 2026' and that 'the true speedup could be much higher among the developers/tasks selected out of the experiment.' So METR reads its weak evidence as pointing toward a real-but-unmeasurable speedup, not toward 'no speedup.' Presenting it purely as 'no robust proof of speedup' inverts METR's directional conclusion. Honest read: evidence is too weak to size the effect, but METR itself leans positive.

CLAIM 6 currency — the Microsoft/MIT/Princeton/Wharton 3-RCT (+26.08% PRs/week) ran in 2022-2023 on a GPT-3.5-based autocomplete Copilot. Per this project's own rule (pre-2025 = largely obsolete), it should be used ONLY as a historical autocomplete-era upper bound, not as agentic-era evidence. The claim flags it as 'pre-agentic' (good) but still lists it among current evidence; for a C-level deck it is ~3 years stale and tool-generation-obsolete. The Accenture-specific sub-figures (+8.7% PRs/dev, +84% builds) are NOT in the cited InfoQ article.
corrected_numbers: Faros 'code churn ~10x increase' → actual figure is +861% (~9.6x). 'About 10x' is loosely defensible but the precise, citable number is +861%. Source: faros.ai whiplash takeaways.

Faros 'median review time ~5x' → confirmed as +441.5% (≈5.4x). Use +441.5%. Note Faros also reports median-time-to-first-review +156.6% and average-time-in-review +199.6% — three different review-time metrics that should not be conflated.

Faros methodology caveat (affects ALL Faros numbers): gains and penalties are measured by comparing 'periods of LOWEST vs HIGHEST AI adoption within each organization,' not a clean same-team-same-period A/B. And Faros IS a vendor — it sells an engineering-intelligence/governance platform, and the 'whiplash/governance-gap' narrative directly markets that product. The claim calls it 'NOT vendor-marketing' — technically true (not a coding-tool vendor) but it is still vendor-authored content with a product-aligned thesis. Data is from Faros customers (selection bias).

METR 2026 cohort detail: the '-4% new recruits' is from a combined updated cohort of 57 developers (10 original + 47 new) across 143 repos and 800+ tasks — worth stating precisely so it isn't read as 47 clean new devs.

DORA 2025 stability caveat: throughput reversed to POSITIVE, but DORA 2025 still finds AI adoption has a NEGATIVE relationship with delivery STABILITY (instability persists, just is now better managed by strong-platform teams). CLAIM 4 emphasizes the throughput reversal but under-states that the stability penalty did NOT fully reverse in 2025 — directly relevant to a risk-averse bank.

Stack Overflow 2025: the '66%' figure is 'spend more time fixing almost-right AI code,' while the '45%' is the share citing 'almost right but not quite' as their top frustration — CLAIM 8 slightly conflates the two. Both are real. Trust-in-accuracy fell 40%→29% YoY; favorability 72%→60%; distrust 46% > trust 33%; only 3% 'highly trust.' All confirmed.

Contradicting-evidence calibration: independent Gartner 2026 puts NET enterprise productivity gain at ~19.3% — which sits INSIDE the skeptical 10-25% system-level band, NOT the '2-10x' vendor headline. The large numbers (Stanford 71%, Morgan Stanley 280k hours, Klarna $60M, 171% ROI) are vendor/'successful-deployment' case studies (survivorship + narrow tasks like legacy-code translation), so they reinforce rather than refute the research's core thesis.
verdict.notes:
VERDICT: mostly_solid. The headline numbers are real and accurately sourced; the framing has two genuine misattributions (Bain/Amdahl) and one directional spin (METR) that a CIO should not be shown uncorrected.

WHAT HOLDS UP WELL:
- METR 2025 RCT (-19% slowdown, ~39pt perception gap): verified, primary source, gold-standard design. The single strongest counter-narrative and it survives scrutiny.
- METR May 2026 follow-up survey (NEW, not in claims, worth ADDING): self-reported median ~3x speedup vs. measured -4 to -18% — the 40-point perception-vs-reality gap PERSISTS into 2026. This strengthens the 'trust the telemetry, not the vibes' thesis and is the most decision-relevant fresh data point.
- Faros numbers: all verified to the primary source (with churn corrected to +861%). The 'more throughput + more bugs/incidents/review-debt' tradeoff is the most decision-relevant pattern for a bank — but apply the vendor + methodology caveats above.
- DORA 2024 (-1.5% throughput, -7.2% stability per +25pp) and DORA 2025 (90% adoption, throughput reversal positive, stability still negative, 'amplifier not fixer'): both verified.
- Stack Overflow 2025 (adoption up, trust/favorability down): verified.
- Anthropic 2026 agentic-vs-autocomplete shift (session 4→23 min, multi-file 34%→78%, delegation gap 0-20%): verified — but it is VENDOR data; use for the qualitative agentic/autocomplete distinction, not as a productivity proof point.

NET FOR THE CIO: The honest, defensible story is NOT '10x developers' and NOT 'AI makes devs slower, full stop.' It is: (a) rigorous independent measurement shows real-world net gains are modest at the SYSTEM level — roughly 10-25%, with Gartner's independent ~19% landing squarely in that band; (b) raw coding throughput genuinely rises 30-65% but that surplus migrates downstream into MORE bugs (+54%), MORE incidents (up to ~3x per PR), and a MASSIVELY strained review process (+441% median review time, 31% of PRs merged unreviewed) unless controls exist first; (c) practitioner trust is FALLING even as usage rises; (d) the perception-reality gap is large and persistent. For a regulated Swiss bank the load-bearing message is the Faros/DORA 'acceleration whiplash + amplifier' finding: AI pays off ONLY where strong testing, review, and platform discipline already exist — exactly the controls a bank should fund BEFORE seats. Two framing fixes required before this goes in a deck: (1) relabel the Amdahl/'unremarkable'/'six studies' line as independent-analyst synthesis, not a Bain finding; (2) present METR 2026 as 'too-weak-to-size, METR itself leans positive' rather than 'no proof of speedup.'"

findings.dimension: Token Economics & Cost — what agentic coding actually costs in tokens/compute vs. developer salaries (esp. Swiss/Raiffeisen scale of several hundred devs)

key_findings.claim: At enterprise scale, blended Claude Code token spend averages ~$150-$250 per developer per month (~$13/active developer-day), with 90% of users under $12/day. Vendor (Anthropic) self-reported.
key_findings.evidence: Anthropic enterprise data: '$150-$250 per developer per month average'; 'average ~$6 per developer per day, 90% of users spending under $12 daily ($360/month at ceiling)'. EU equivalent quoted at EUR 100-250/month for daily agentic users.

key_findings.claim: Against a Swiss fully-loaded developer cost (~CHF 120-160k+ salary, ~CHF 140-200k loaded), typical agentic token spend of $150-330/month is roughly 1-3% of total developer cost. Break-even needs only ~3 saved hours/month.
key_findings.evidence: Average SW engineer Zurich CHF 125-130k TC (senior ~CHF 144k). Palma: AI tooling = 1-3% of $150-250k loaded dev cost; '3.2 hours of saved developer time per month' to break even at $300/dev/month vs $94/hr. Swiss employer social load is LOW (~6-10% vs Germany ~20%), so loaded cost is closer to gross than in EU.

key_findings.claim: Per-task cost has FALLEN sharply: Claude Opus 4.5 (Nov 2025) cut prices 67% AND used ~76% fewer output tokens for equivalent work — a roughly order-of-magnitude drop in cost-per-completed-task in one release. Opus is now $5/$25 per MTok vs Opus 4.1's $15/$75.
key_findings.evidence: Opus 4 / 4.1 = $15 in / $75 out per MTok; Opus 4.5-4.8 = $5 in / $25 out. '67% price cut combined with 76% fewer output tokens for equivalent work'. Launched Nov 24 2025.
key_findings.date: Nov 24 2025; pricing confirmed on platform.claude.com June 2026

key_findings.claim: BUT total enterprise AI spend is rising fast (Jevons paradox): per-token prices fell ~10x/yr (Epoch: median 50x/yr, 200x/yr post-2024 for fixed capability) yet total spend rose ~320% over the same window because agentic workflows burn 5-1000x more tokens than chat.
key_findings.evidence: Epoch AI: GPT-4-class price fell ~40x/yr; LLM inference '10x annually as of Dec 2025'. Counter-trend: 'token prices fell 280x over two years, but total enterprise AI spend rose 320%'. Agentic tasks consume 1000x more tokens than code chat (Microsoft Research).

key_findings.claim: A single agentic coding session (~50 turns) costs roughly $0.60-$6.00 depending on model; input tokens dominate (85% of cost, ~20-25x more input than output). Cost-per-PR-review ~$0.72 vs ~$48 senior-engineer time.
key_findings.evidence: Vantage: 50-turn session = ~1M input + 40k output tokens. Opus 4.6 $6.00, GPT-5.4 $3.10, Composer 2 Fast $1.80, Composer 2 Standard $0.60. GitHub/Anthropic vendor data: agent PR review $0.72 vs $48 human (66x); unit-test gen $0.51 vs $32 (63x).

key_findings.claim: Heavy/power users and autonomous runs blow past averages dramatically and are HARD to forecast — the key budgeting risk. Uber spent its ENTIRE 2026 AI coding budget in 4 months; Microsoft canceled most direct Claude Code licenses 6 months after launch over scale cost.
key_findings.evidence: Uber: $500-$2,000/engineer/month, 95% of engineers use AI monthly, 70% of committed code is AI-generated, 'back to the drawing board' on budgeting (Apr 17 2026). Pragmatic Engineer: one engineer spent $1,400 in a single day; some devs $500/day; another hit $4,200 over a long weekend on an autonomous refactor. Run-to-run token use varies up to 30x on identical tasks; models underestimate their own token cost (correlation only 0.39).
key_findings.date: Uber Apr 17 2026 / Pragmatic Engineer 2026 / Microsoft Research Apr 2026

key_findings.claim: The whole industry is converging on usage-based (token) billing — Raiffeisen cannot avoid token economics by buying flat-rate seats. GitHub Copilot moved to token-based billing June 1 2026; flat seat fee now just buys a credit allotment, overages metered.
key_findings.evidence: Copilot Enterprise stays $39/seat but now includes only $39 of AI Credits; overage $0.01/credit, billed on input+output+cached tokens at model API rates. Cursor Team $40/seat, Windsurf Teams $40/seat, Devin $2.25/ACU pay-as-you-go. All major tools now meter usage on top of (or instead of) seats.

key_findings.claim: ROI on agentic coding is real but back-loaded and not universal — engineering has the SLOWEST payback of agent use cases. Independent benchmark: 9.3-month median payback for engineering; only ~40% of engineering rollouts hit positive ROI within 12 months; 19% never reach payback.
key_findings.evidence: Bain Agentic AI Benchmark 2026 (independent, n=1,840): payback 4.1mo customer service, 6.7mo marketing, 9.3mo engineering. '40% of engineering deployments hit positive ROI within 12 months vs 63% for customer service'; '19% never reach payback'. Healthy ROI 2.5-3.5x, top quartile 4-6x.

pro_arguments: Token cost is a tiny fraction of a Swiss developer's loaded cost: at $150-330/dev/month it is ~1-3% of a CHF 140-200k+ loaded engineer. Break-even requires only ~3 saved hours/month (under 1 hour/week). Even conservative 10% productivity gains imply 3-5x ROI; typical gains 8-15x. (Palma, Feb 2026)

Cost-per-completed-task is collapsing, not rising. The Opus 4.5 release (Nov 2025) cut per-token price 67% AND used 76% fewer output tokens — roughly an order-of-magnitude drop in cost per finished task in a single model generation. Per-token prices for fixed capability fall ~10x/year (Epoch). Budgeting on today's unit cost is conservative.

Cost is highly controllable with known levers: model routing (Haiku $1/$5, Sonnet $3/$15 vs Opus $5/$25), prompt caching (cache reads at 10% of input price — pays off after one reuse), and the Batch API (50% off). One SaaS firm cut spend ~30% just by defaulting to Sonnet. For a bank, most code work runs fine on Sonnet, reserving Opus for hard reasoning.

At Raiffeisen's scale a credible all-in budget is bounded and modellable: ~$1.9-4.0M/year for 1,000 devs (seats + MCP + governance + ops), so roughly $1-2M/year for several hundred devs — a rounding error against a several-hundred-developer payroll of well over CHF 50-80M.

The whole market has standardized on usage-based pricing (Copilot went token-metered June 1 2026; Cursor, Windsurf, Devin all meter usage), which means costs are transparent, attributable per team/cost-center, and capped via budget controls — exactly the governance a FINMA-regulated bank needs to monitor third-party spend.

Concrete per-task economics are favorable even at vendor-optimistic best case: ~$0.72 per agent PR review vs ~$48 of senior-engineer time, $0.51 vs $32 for unit-test generation. Even discounting these 3-5x for rework, the unit economics favor the agent for repetitive, well-scoped tasks.
contra_arguments: Spend is elastic and very hard to forecast — the single biggest financial risk. Uber burned its ENTIRE 2026 AI coding budget in 4 months and went 'back to the drawing board.' Individual blow-ups are common: $1,400 in a day, $500/day per dev, $4,200 over one weekend on an autonomous refactor. Identical tasks vary up to 30x in token use run-to-run, and models underestimate their own cost (corr. only 0.39) — so bottom-up budgeting is unreliable without hard caps.

Cheaper tokens do NOT mean cheaper AI: total enterprise spend rose ~320% over two years even as per-token prices fell 280x (Jevons paradox). Agentic workflows burn 5-1000x more tokens than chat. Without strict guardrails, savings from price cuts are immediately consumed by more autonomous, longer-running agent loops.

Even Microsoft and Nvidia signal the cost ceiling: Microsoft canceled most direct Claude Code licenses ~6 months after launch over scale cost; Nvidia's Bryan Catanzaro: 'the cost of compute is far beyond the costs of the employees' for his team. For heavy senior agentic users, token spend already exceeds 20% of fully-loaded cost — and can rival or exceed a salary.

ROI in engineering is the slowest and least certain of all agent use cases: 9.3-month median payback, only ~40% of engineering rollouts positive within 12 months, and 19% NEVER reach payback (Bain 2026, independent). Vague productivity claims should be discounted by a ~60% utilization factor plus rework cost on AI-generated code.

Most flattering per-task figures ($0.72/PR vs $48 human; 66x cheaper) come from VENDORS (Anthropic, GitHub) selling the product and exclude the cost of human review, rework, and security/compliance checks that a bank must add on top of every AI change — eroding the headline multiplier.

Banking-specific cost adders are not in the consumer pricing: data-residency / US-only inference adds a 1.1x multiplier; regional Bedrock/Vertex endpoints add ~10%; governance + evaluation infra is projected to rise from 18-24% to 28-34% of the agent program budget by mid-2027 as compliance hardens. Real Raiffeisen unit cost will be meaningfully above the sticker token price.
findings.confidence_notes: Strongest, most defensible numbers: Anthropic API price table (primary source, platform.claude.com, June 2026) and the GitHub Copilot June 1 2026 billing shift (primary GitHub blog). The Opus 4.5 67% cut + 76% fewer output tokens is well-corroborated (the-decoder, multiple outlets, Nov 2025). Epoch AI price-decline trend is a credible independent research source. WEAK / VENDOR-BIASED: the $150-250/dev/month blended figure and the $0.72-vs-$48 per-task multipliers are Anthropic/GitHub self-reported (best case, exclude review/rework) — flag as vendor marketing. The Bain payback figures (9.3mo, 40%, 19% never) are the most useful INDEPENDENT counterweight but I could not open the primary Bain report; cited via a secondary aggregator (digitalapplied) — verify the original before quoting to the CIO. Uber 4-month-budget and Microsoft license-cancellation are reported via secondary outlets (briefs.co, Fortune) citing internal sources, not company filings — directionally reliable, exact dollar totals not disclosed. Swiss salary range (CHF 117-130k avg, senior ~144k) is solid from multiple 2026 salary trackers; note Swiss employer social load is unusually LOW (~6-10%), so 'fully loaded' is closer to gross than EU/US norms — this slightly worsens the token-as-%-of-cost ratio vs US examples but tokens remain a small single-digit % for typical use. Run-to-run 30x variance and 'models underestimate own cost' come from a peer-reviewed-track Microsoft Research/OpenReview paper (Apr 2026) — high confidence on the qualitative risk, exact absolute token counts not in the abstract. Overall: the PRO case (tokens are cheap vs Swiss salaries, falling per unit) and the CONTRA case (uncontrolled elastic spend, slow engineering payback, vendor-inflated per-task math) are BOTH well-supported; the deciding variable for Raiffeisen is governance/budget-controls, not headline price.

Anthropic DOUBLED its per-dev estimate from $6/day to $13/day around mid-April 2026 (letsdatascience.com). The brief's own '90% under $12/day' figure understates the budgeting tail by ~2.5x — a material error for a CIO sizing worst-case spend. CRITICAL: ALL Claim 1 figures are Anthropic self-reported vendor data with no independent audit.

CLAIM 5 OVERTURNED on the $0.72-per-PR-review figure: This sub-dollar number could NOT be traced to any primary GitHub Octoverse or Anthropic source despite the brief attributing it to 'GitHub/Anthropic vendor data.' It is a blog aggregation (digitalapplied.com) with no primary URL. Anthropic's ACTUAL shipped Code Review feature is reported at $15-25 per pull request (InfoQ, Apr 2026) — 20-35x higher than the claimed $0.72. The '66x cheaper than human' headline collapses if the real per-PR cost is $15-25 vs a $48 human cost (~2-3x, not 66x). The per-session $0.60-$6.00 range (Claim 5) IS reasonable but is Vantage's own illustrative estimate, not measured vendor data.

The '70%' figure conflates 'AI-assisted/AI-touched code' with 'autonomous-agent code' — very different metrics. The COO (Macdonald) explicitly questioned ROI: 'That link is not there yet.' The headline (entire 2026 AI budget burned in 4 months, $1,500/month cap, $500-2,000/eng/month) IS confirmed by Fortune/multiple outlets — this is a STRONG cautionary data point for Raiffeisen, but the '70% AI-generated' stat should be dropped or recaptioned.

The actual Bain article ('Your AI Budget Is Growing, Your Returns Aren't,' bain.com) cites n=951 companies and contains NO function-level payback breakdown — its headline finding is that ~40% of firms measuring savings landed BELOW 10% (worse than targeted). The 9.3-month/n=1,840 numbers exist ONLY in a secondary marketing blog (digitalapplied.com) with no Bain URL. The directional message (engineering = slowest payback, ROI back-loaded) is plausible and consistent with the real Bain finding that returns disappoint, but the specific numbers are UNVERIFIED and the two cited sample sizes (951 vs 1,840) are inconsistent.

Epoch price decline: the brief's headline '~10x/year' is the LLM-inference figure; the per-benchmark range is 9x-900x/yr with a 50x/yr MEDIAN and 40x/yr for GPT-4-class capability. Composer/GPT/Opus per-session costs ($0.60-$6.00) are Vantage's illustrative estimates (1M input + 40k output, input = ~85% of cost), NOT measured — label as modeled, not empirical.
verdict.notes:
VERDICT: mostly_solid. The CORE economic thesis is robust and well-supported by PRIMARY sources: (a) per-token prices have fallen sharply (Epoch AI primary, confirmed: 9x-900x/yr, median 50x, GPT-4-class 40x/yr); (b) Opus 4.5 cut prices 67% to $5/$25 per MTok AND used 76% fewer output tokens (Anthropic primary, Nov 24 2025 — confirmed); (c) Jevons-paradox dynamic is REAL and the strongest, best-sourced part of the brief — the Microsoft Research paper (arXiv 2604.22750, 'How Do AI Agents Spend Your Money?') is a genuine PRIMARY academic source confirming agentic tasks consume ~1000x more tokens than chat, input dominates cost, runs vary up to 30x on identical tasks, and models underestimate their own token cost (note: the 0.39 self-prediction correlation and 30x variance trace to THIS paper, NOT to Pragmatic Engineer as the brief cites); (d) the industry HAS converged on usage-based billing — GitHub Copilot's June 1 2026 move to AI-credits/token metering is confirmed from GitHub's own blog and is already causing 'meter shock' (Visual Studio Magazine: dev facing $180 June bill). (e) Swiss salary anchor is sound: Zurich senior SWE ~CHF 140-154k median (Levels.fyi/Glassdoor 2026), and at ~CHF 140-200k loaded, $150-330/month tooling is ~1-3% — the break-even of ~3 saved hours/month is arithmetically correct.

KEY ADVERSARIAL CAVEATS FOR THE CIO:
1. VENDOR-BIAS CONCENTRATION: The most reassuring numbers (cost-per-dev, $0.72/PR, ROI multiples) are vendor or vendor-adjacent (Anthropic, Palma.ai — which SELLS MCP cost-governance, GitHub, digitalapplied marketing blog). The most ALARMING numbers (Uber budget blowout, Microsoft dropping Claude Code, heavy-user $500-$2,000/month, $4,200/weekend) come from independent journalism (Fortune, Pragmatic Engineer, multiple outlets) and PRIMARY academic work (Microsoft Research). When the bad news is better-sourced than the good news, default to the bad news for budgeting.
2. THE TAIL IS THE RISK, AND IT'S BIGGER THAN CLAIMED. The brief's '90% under $12/day' is wrong ($30/day is the real 90th percentile per Anthropic) — and even that ceiling is for 90%, leaving a 10% power-user tail at $500-2,000/month. With 'several hundred devs,' Raiffeisen should budget for a fat tail, not the $150-250 average. Both Uber AND Microsoft — sophisticated buyers — blew their annual budgets in months because usage scales with usefulness. Hard per-seat caps and metered governance are non-optional.
3. ROI IS BACK-LOADED AND NOT UNIVERSAL — and the real Bain study is actually MORE skeptical than the brief: ~40% of firms that measured savings landed below 10%, under their 11-20% target. Even if the 9.3-month engineering-payback figure is unverified, the directional caution (engineering = slowest, returns disappoint) is corroborated by primary Bain.
4. NET FRAMING FOR THE CIO: At blended averages the math is overwhelmingly favorable (~1-3% of loaded dev cost; break-even ~3 hrs/month). The risk is NOT average cost — it is (i) unbudgeted power-user/autonomous-run tails, (ii) the structural Jevons trap where better tools cost more, and (iii) vendor lock-in to usage-based billing you cannot escape with flat seats. SWISS/REGULATORY angle not directly covered by these claims but adjacent: usage-based token billing routed through Anthropic/GitHub/Bedrock raises FINMA outsourcing, EU AI Act, and data-residency questions that should be a separate dimension. Recommend: present averages AND the documented blowout cases side-by-side; insist on per-seat/workspace spend caps (Anthropic supports workspace limits) from day one; treat any sub-dollar per-task ROI multiple as marketing until validated on Raiffeisen's own pilot telemetry.

findings.dimension: Developer Headcount: Does agentic coding reduce, hold flat, or increase the number of developers needed?

key_findings.claim: The empirical net signal in 2026 points UP, not down: aggregate software-engineering demand is rising despite mass AI adoption. Software engineer job postings on Indeed are up ~11% year-over-year (early 2026), faster than postings overall, with ~67,000 open SWE positions in Q1 2026 - the highest since early 2023.
key_findings.evidence: Citadel Securities analysis of Indeed data: SWE postings 'rapidly rising,' +11% YoY; ~67,000 open SWE positions Q1 2026 (highest since early 2023); IT/CS postings +14.2% YoY in April 2026. AI/ML engineer postings up ~85% YoY.

key_findings.claim: This is the Jevons paradox in action: cheaper code raises total demand for code. Cheaper/faster development makes previously unjustifiable projects viable, expanding the work backlog faster than productivity removes it. Gartner projects worldwide IT spending of $6.15 trillion in 2026, +10.8% YoY, with AI the dominant driver - more software being built, not less.
key_findings.evidence: Gartner 2026 IT spend forecast $6.15T (+10.8% YoY). 'AI makes software development 2x-10x faster, which makes thousands of previously unjustifiable projects economically viable' - the core Jevons mechanism. ~60% of new enterprise software projects in 2026 include an agentic component.

key_findings.claim: The composition of headcount is shifting sharply even where the total holds or grows: junior/entry-level hiring is collapsing while senior and AI-specialist demand surges. This is the single most important nuance for a CIO: the same total headcount may need a very different skill mix.
key_findings.evidence: Share of juniors/graduates in IT employment dropped from ~15% to ~7% over three years. Entry-level tech hiring -25% YoY in 2024; some report junior hiring down ~50%. Developers aged 22-25 lost ~20% of positions since ChatGPT launched. A 2025 LeadDev survey found 54% of engineering leaders plan to hire fewer juniors. Meanwhile ML engineer salaries +35%, AI/ML postings +85% YoY, and 'AI Engineer' is LinkedIn's #1 fastest-growing US job title in 2026.

key_findings.claim: Big Tech is explicitly trading some engineering headcount for AI productivity - but mostly freezing/redeploying rather than mass-firing engineers. Salesforce did NOT expand its software-developer workforce in FY2026, citing AI agents; Benioff says AI improved engineering productivity ~30%. CAUTION: Salesforce's headline 4,000 job cuts were in customer SUPPORT (9,000 to 5,000), NOT engineering.
key_findings.evidence: Benioff: Salesforce will not expand developer headcount in FY2026 due to AI agents; AI lifted engineering productivity ~30%; 'AI is already doing 30-50% of Salesforce's work' (engineering, coding, support). Support headcount cut from 9,000 to ~5,000 (4,000 roles), described as 'rebalance,' hundreds redeployed to sales/services. Separately hiring 1,000 new grads/interns to build AI.

key_findings.claim: Amazon's CEO is the clearest C-level voice projecting AI-driven workforce SHRINKAGE - but hedged and partly walked back. Andy Jassy told employees AI will reduce Amazon's total corporate workforce in coming years; Amazon cut ~30,000 corporate jobs (~10% of white-collar) in Oct 2025. He later muddied attribution, saying the cuts were about 'culture,' not AI/cost.
key_findings.evidence: Jassy: 'we will need fewer people doing some of the jobs being done today, and more people doing other types of jobs... in the next few years we expect that this will reduce our total corporate workforce.' But also: 'It's hard to know exactly where this nets out.' And Nov 2025: layoffs were 'about culture,' not AI. ~30,000 corporate cuts Oct 2025; >27,000 cut since 2022.

key_findings.claim: AI now writes a large minority of code at Big Tech, yet engineer headcounts at those same firms have NOT collapsed - a key 'output up at flat headcount' signal rather than wholesale replacement. Microsoft: AI writes 20-30% of code (Nadella, Apr 2025). Google: >30% of new code AI-generated (Pichai, Apr 2025).
key_findings.evidence: Nadella: 20-30% of Microsoft code AI-written, some projects nearly all. Pichai: >30% of new Google code AI-generated. Zuckerberg: AI could do the work of Meta's mid-level engineers in 2025 (but stressed human creativity remains). Despite this, core engineering headcounts at these firms have not dropped proportionally - the productivity is absorbed by more output.

key_findings.claim: INDEPENDENT, peer-style evidence undercuts the 'AI = fewer devs needed' productivity premise. The METR RCT (July 2025) found experienced open-source developers were 19% SLOWER with early-2025 AI tools on mature codebases they knew well - despite believing AI sped them up ~20%. If real-world senior productivity gains are smaller/negative than vendors claim, headcount-reduction business cases are overstated.
key_findings.evidence: METR RCT: 16 experienced devs, 246 tasks, avg 5 yrs on their repos, using Cursor Pro + Claude 3.5/3.7. Result: AI-allowed tasks took 19% LONGER. Devs forecast 24% speedup beforehand, estimated 20% speedup after - a stark perception-reality gap. Published July 2025 (arXiv 2507.09089).

key_findings.claim: Stanford's large-scale study (100,000+ devs, 600+ companies) shows productivity gains are real but modest and highly variable - NOT the 2x-10x vendors imply - and warns headcount-cut logic often fails. This supports holding headcount and raising output over cutting headcount.
key_findings.evidence: Stanford 3-year study, 100,000+ engineers, 600+ companies: AI lifts productivity ~15-20% on average (median 10-15%; skilled teams 20-30%; weak teams near-zero or negative). Greenfield/simple tasks: 30-40% gains; complex mature codebases in less-popular languages: can DECREASE productivity. 'Cut a percentage of engineers and expect AI to make up the difference... the research suggests this approach may not yield expected results.'

key_findings.claim: Google's 2025 DORA report (90% of devs now use AI) found AI adoption is now linked to HIGHER delivery throughput (a reversal of 2024), but with a persistent NEGATIVE relationship to delivery stability - meaning more code volume without strong controls raises defect/instability risk. For a bank, this argues for headcount in review/QA/platform, not just code generation.
key_findings.evidence: DORA 2025: 90% of dev professionals use AI (+14pts YoY), median 2 hrs/day; >80% report productivity gains. AI now POSITIVELY linked to throughput (reversal of 2024). BUT AI adoption still has a NEGATIVE relationship with delivery stability. 'AI amplifies what's already there' - strong teams improve, weak teams' problems intensify.

key_findings.claim: The Klarna case is the most-cited 'AI reversal' - but it is a CUSTOMER SERVICE story, not coding. It is frequently misused as evidence against agentic engineering. The honest read: it warns against over-automating quality-sensitive work, which is relevant to code review/QA, but it is NOT evidence that agentic CODING fails.
key_findings.evidence: Klarna laid off ~700 (10% of staff) for an AI assistant handling 75% of chats (2.3M conversations). By 2025-2026 CEO Siemiatkowski admitted 'we went too far... focused too much on efficiency and cost. The result was lower quality' and began rehiring humans into a hybrid model. This was support, not software engineering.

key_findings.claim: New dedicated roles are exploding - directly justifying the CIO's second ask (dedicated personnel units, not just tools). Agentic-AI job postings +280% YoY (~90,000 US listings); forward-deployed engineer listings +800% in 2025. New titles: AI Engineer, AI/Agent Orchestrator, RAG Engineer, AI Guardian, MLOps - the people who keep agents from drifting, conflicting, or failing in production.
key_findings.evidence: Agentic-AI postings +280% YoY (~90,000 US listings); forward-deployed engineer +800% (2025). ML Engineer category +41.8% (fastest-growing). Korn Ferry 2026 (1,674 talent leaders): 52% plan to deploy autonomous AI agents by end-2026. Highest salary premiums: multi-agent orchestration, RAG, LangChain, vector DBs.

key_findings.claim: Swiss/banking-specific signal: headcount moves at Swiss banks are dominated by restructuring/offshoring, not AI productivity alone - but AI is the stated rationale for shifting tech work to lower-cost hubs. UBS is cutting ~3,000 Swiss jobs (and ~10,000 total by 2027) while DOUBLING its Hyderabad, India headcount in tech/engineering/AI. For Raiffeisen, this signals AI enables relocating, not just eliminating, engineering capacity - a governance/data-residency consideration.

Simultaneously 'aims to double headcount in Hyderabad... focusing on technology, engineering and AI.' Much of the Swiss cut is Credit Suisse merger overlap, not pure AI.

pro_arguments: Net demand is UP, not down: SWE postings +11% YoY in 2026, ~67,000 open positions (highest since 2023). The Jevons paradox is empirically showing - cheaper/faster code unlocks a larger backlog of viable projects, so total engineering work expands. Investing in agentic coding positions Raiffeisen to capture that expanded output, not to shrink the team.

The realistic model is 'same (or modestly fewer) developers producing far more,' not mass layoffs. Big Tech proves it: Microsoft/Google have 20-30%+ of code AI-written yet did not proportionally cut engineers - the productivity is absorbed as more shipped software. For a bank with a large project backlog, this means faster delivery at flat headcount.

Tools alone are not enough - the data justifies dedicated personnel units. Agentic-AI roles +280% YoY, forward-deployed/AI engineers +800%, and entirely new titles (AI/agent orchestrator, RAG engineer, AI guardian, MLOps) are now the fastest-growing, highest-premium roles. A dedicated agentic-engineering unit is exactly what high performers are staffing.

DORA 2025 (90% AI adoption) shows AI now lifts delivery throughput - a reversal of the negative 2024 finding - when paired with strong platform/testing/version-control practices. Raiffeisen can realistically expect more releases per quarter at current headcount IF it invests in the surrounding engineering discipline (which a dedicated unit provides).

Retaining and up-skilling SENIOR engineers becomes more valuable, not less: gains concentrate in skilled teams (20-30%) and evaporate or go negative in weak teams. Investment in agentic coding doubles as a retention/up-skilling lever for Raiffeisen's existing senior talent - the people who turn agents into leverage.
contra_arguments: Independent evidence undercuts the headline productivity claims. The METR RCT found experienced developers 19% SLOWER with AI on mature codebases they know well - the exact profile of a bank's legacy core-banking code. Vendor 30%+ and CEO 'AI does 30-50% of our work' figures are self-reported and likely overstated for complex, regulated codebases. A headcount-reduction business case built on vendor numbers is fragile.

Real, AI-attributed reductions ARE happening - the CIO should not be told 'AI never cuts jobs.' Amazon cut ~30,000 corporate roles (Jassy: AI will 'reduce our total corporate workforce'); Salesforce froze developer hiring for FY2026 and cut 4,000 support roles; Meta traded 600 AI roles for compute. The honest framing is: AI shifts and can shrink headcount, especially juniors - it does not uniformly grow teams.

The junior pipeline is collapsing (junior share 15% to 7%, entry hiring -25% to -50%). If Raiffeisen leans hard into agents, it risks the same trap: no junior intake means no senior pipeline in 5-10 years, and seniors are precisely who you need to review agent output. This is a structural, slow-burn risk an over-eager investment can worsen.

The most-cited 'reversal' (Klarna) was over-automation of QUALITY-sensitive work, and it backfired ('we went too far... lower quality... not sustainable' - rehired humans). For a bank, code review, security, and QA are the quality-sensitive layer. Cutting human review headcount to ride agent output could reproduce Klarna's mistake in a regulated, defect-intolerant environment. DORA's negative AI-stability link reinforces this.

Headcount 'savings' at peers often mean OFFSHORING, not net elimination - UBS is cutting ~3,000 Swiss jobs while doubling its India tech/AI hub. For Raiffeisen the relevant lever may be relocation, which collides with FINMA outsourcing rules, data residency, and Swiss cooperative-bank labor/political sensitivities. The pure 'fewer developers, lower cost' narrative is not cleanly available to a Swiss bank.

Much of the 2026 hiring 'rebound' data and the strongest Jevons claims come from recruiting firms, vendors (Anthropic's 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report is gated marketing), and tech-CEO statements - all with incentives to sell optimism. The genuinely independent studies (METR, Stanford) are more sober: modest, highly variable gains, not transformation.
findings.confidence_notes: STRONG independent anchors: METR RCT (arXiv 2507.09089, peer-grade methodology) and Stanford's 100k-dev/600-company study are the most credible and both temper vendor hype (modest/variable gains; 19% slowdown on mature code). DORA 2025 is Google-published but methodologically respected and notably NOT pro-AI on stability. WEAKER/vendor-biased: the '+11% YoY / 67,000 openings' rebound and Jevons-paradox framing are amplified by recruiting firms (jobsbyculture, herohunt, secondtalent), Marc Andreessen (an AI investor), and blogs; the underlying Indeed/Citadel and TrueUp data are real but the optimistic interpretation is interested. Anthropic's 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report is gated vendor marketing - I could not extract its hard numbers (form-gated) and would not cite its figures without the primary PDF. CEO statements (Benioff 30%, 'AI does 30-50% of work'; Nadella/Pichai code-share %; Jassy) are self-reported and partly contradictory (Jassy attributed Amazon cuts to AI in June, then to 'culture' in November) - treat as directional, not measured. CRITICAL FRAMING RISK to flag to the CIO: the two most-cited 'AI failure/reversal' cases (Klarna, Salesforce's 4,000 cuts) are CUSTOMER SUPPORT, not software engineering - they are routinely misapplied to coding. The junior-collapse numbers vary widely by source (-25% to -50%) and mix causes (AI + 2022-2024 macro tech downturn + rate environment), so AI's isolated causal share is genuinely uncertain. Swiss-specific developer-headcount data is thin; UBS is the main local datapoint and is dominated by the Credit Suisse merger, not AI - extrapolate to Raiffeisen with caution. Net honest read: evidence does NOT support 'agentic coding lets you cut developers'; it supports 'flat-to-growing headcount with a shifted skill mix (more senior/AI-specialist, fewer juniors) and more output' - contingent on investing in review/QA/platform discipline and dedicated agent-engineering roles.

verdict.dimension: Developer Headcount: Does agentic coding reduce, hold flat, or increase the number of developers needed?
overturned_claims: Claim 1/2 'empirical net signal points UP, demand is rising': MATERIALLY MISLEADING by omission. The same Indeed dataset the findings cite shows general software-engineering postings remain ~49% BELOW their pre-pandemic baseline, and tech postings overall are down ~one-third from pre-pandemic (CIO Dive / Indeed Hiring Lab; Pragmatic Engineer 2026). The +11% YoY is a rebound off a deep 2023-24 trough, not net expansion, and is concentrated in AI/ML/security (ML postings +59% ABOVE pre-pandemic) while general SWE stays deeply depressed. Pragmatic Engineer: listings 'still lower than May 2021.' Presenting +11% as proof demand is structurally UP is cherry-picking.

Claim 1/2 omits the largest contradicting fact: ~142,000-148,000 tech layoffs in 2026 by early June (Crunchbase/TechTimes/Yahoo Finance), on pace for ~370,000 for the year; Tom's Hardware reports ~50% of Q1 2026 cuts were attributed to AI. A headcount briefing that argues 'net signal UP' while omitting the biggest layoff wave on record is not balanced. (Caveat both ways: several analysts argue these are cost-discipline/hiring-freeze, not pure AI substitution.)

Claim 7 (METR -19%): now ONE-SIDED. METR's own 2026-02-24 update reports their late-2025 follow-up data showed a REVERSAL (~-18%, i.e. a speedup, for original devs) and explicitly warns the July 2025 -19% result 'may be outdated' due to selection bias (devs increasingly refused to work without AI; 30-50% avoided submitting AI-suited tasks). METR is redesigning the experiment. Citing only the -19% headline without the Feb 2026 walkback overstates the anti-productivity evidence.

Claim 2 Jevons framing via Gartner $6.15T is weakly supported as a SOFTWARE/labor argument: the spend surge is dominated by AI hardware/infrastructure (data centers +31.7%, servers +36.9%, GenAI models +80.8%), while software spend grows only +14.7%. Most of the $6.15T is not 'more application software being built by more developers.' Also stale: Gartner revised the figure UP to $6.31T / +13.5% in April 2026.
corrected_numbers: Junior-share '~15% to ~7% over three years' (Claim 3): not what the flagship Stanford 'Canaries in the Coal Mine' study (Brynjolfsson/Chandar/Chen, Nov 2025, ADP payroll, 3.5-5M workers) found. That study found a 13-16% RELATIVE employment decline / ~20% absolute drop for devs aged 22-25, with 35-49 cohort GROWING 6-9%. Separately, Indeed data shows entry-level postings fell from ~8.1% to ~7.4% of the IT mix YoY (not 15%->7%). The '15%->7%' figure appears conflated from a separate CIO.com/UK source; keep the directional point but cite the right study.

Gartner 2026 IT spend: VERIFIED at $6.15T / +10.8% (Gartner press release 2026-02-03, not the blog cited) but SUPERSEDED — revised up to $6.31T / +13.5% on 2026-04-22. Use the primary Gartner source and the updated figure.

Salesforce 4,000 cuts: VERIFIED but the claim's 'NOT AI' framing undersells Benioff's own words — he said the support cuts happened 'because I need less heads' WITH AI (CNBC 2025-09-02). The 'rebalance/redeploy' language is partly Salesforce PR. 'No new engineers hired in FY2026' is confirmed. The ~30% engineering productivity figure is Benioff's own (vendor) claim.

Amazon '30,000' (Claim 5): the CONFIRMED October 2025 round was ~14,000; '30,000' is the reported upper-ceiling total (Fortune/CNN). A further ~16,000 was announced Jan 2026. The 'about culture, not AI' walkback is fully verified (earnings call) — strengthens the claim's own hedge.

UBS Swiss-vs-India (Claim 12): VERIFIED ~3,000 Swiss cuts and a Hyderabad doubling in tech/engineering/AI, BUT UBS explicitly 'has not confirmed' the two are linked and frames the Swiss cuts as Credit Suisse merger overlap in IT/support. The claim's 'AI is the stated rationale for relocating' is slightly overstated — relocation, yes; AI as the stated cause, not officially. Use as a governance/data-residency signal, not as proof AI drives the move.
verdict.notes:
VERDICT: mixed. The core thesis a CIO should take away IS defensible and well-evidenced: agentic coding is NOT producing wholesale developer replacement; the dominant pattern is (a) output up at roughly flat senior headcount, (b) a sharp skill-mix shift away from juniors toward seniors/AI specialists, and (c) genuine explosion of new dedicated roles. The strongest, best-sourced claims: Claim 3 skill-mix shift (Stanford Canaries study, independent ADP payroll data; entry 8.1%->7.4%, senior 38.8%->43.1% of IT mix — corroborated), Claim 6 (Nadella/Pichai AI-code-share + non-collapsing headcount), Claim 8 (Stanford 100k-dev study, ~15-20% net after rework, high variance, explicit 'don't cut and expect AI to backfill' — independent, verified), Claim 9 (DORA 2025 throughput-up-but-stability-negative — verified verbatim, directly supports the bank's case for QA/review/platform headcount), Claim 11 (agentic +280% corroborated by Stanford 2026 AI Index, not just the jobs blog; FDE +800% corroborated by Fast Company).

WHAT'S SHAKY / NEEDS FIXING: The 'demand is rising / net signal UP' framing (Claims 1-2) is the weakest part — it is true off a depressed base but omits that general SWE postings are ~49% below pre-pandemic and that 2026 saw ~142-148k tech layoffs (~half AI-attributed in Q1). For a C-level audience this MUST be presented honestly: the rebound is real but narrow (AI/ML/security), and total tech employment is still contracting. The METR -19% citation needs the Feb 2026 walkback or it overstates the contra case. The Jevons/Gartner argument is real for IT SPEND but is hardware/infra-led, not a clean 'more dev jobs' proof.

VENDOR-BIAS FLAGS: Benioff's ~30% / '30-50% of work' productivity figures are vendor self-reports (Salesforce sells Agentforce) — flag as such. Gartner is independent. METR, Stanford (both studies), DORA, Brynjolfsson/ADP are independent/academic — these are the load-bearing sources and they survive scrutiny. The jobsbyculture.com and spletzer.com blogs cited for headline numbers are weak primary sources; the underlying numbers happen to check out against Gartner/Stanford AI Index, so re-cite to those primaries.

NET FOR THE CIO: 'Hold/grow total, re-mix the skills, add dedicated agent-ops/review roles' is well-supported. 'Cut N engineers because AI' is NOT supported by the independent evidence (METR, Stanford, DORA all caution against it) and the 'demand is booming' optimism is overstated — present both honestly.

findings.dimension: GOVERNANCE — operating model, policies, guardrails and controls for governing agentic coding across several hundred developers in a FINMA-regulated Swiss cooperative bank (Raiffeisen Schweiz)

key_findings.claim: A concrete, auditable governance operating model for agentic coding already exists in the form of a four-phase rollout (Pilot to Guardrails to Scale to Federate) with measurable exit criteria per phase and seven mandatory controls that must be live before scaling.
key_findings.evidence: Phases: Pilot (10-25 engineers, non-restricted repos, single agent, 4-6 wks); Guardrails (same cohort, full control stack, 4-8 wks); Scale (full org, non-restricted repos, license utilization >60%, 8-12 wks); Federate (multiple agents, sensitive repos by exception). Seven mandatory controls = SSO/SCIM, SIEM export, secret scanning, PR gates, license governance, incident response, audit trails. 'What separates deployments that reach scale from the ones that get pulled after a quarter is whether the identity, logging, code review, and incident controls around the agent are in place from day one.'

key_findings.claim: The core regulatory control that satisfies auditors for agentic AI is the 'delegation chain': every agent action must be attributable to a named human authorizer, with that authorization preserved in a tamper-evident (append-only, hash-chained) audit record. This is the single most load-bearing governance primitive.
key_findings.evidence: 'every agent action must be attributable to a human authorizer who defined the scope of what the agent is permitted to do, with that authorization preserved in a tamper-evident audit record.' Technical standard: append-only logs with SHA-256 hash chaining minimum. EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and OWASP LLM Top 10 'converge on one requirement: comprehensive, immutable audit logs.' Implementation: 'Every agent request must map to a human identity through Okta, Entra, or Google Workspace' for audits and offboarding to function.

key_findings.claim: FINMA already has binding governance expectations (Guidance 08/2024) that map directly onto agentic coding: clear allocation of responsibilities, model/system testing, documentation, ancillary controls, training, and explicit third-party/outsourcing controls. FINMA is technology-neutral ('same business, same risks, same rules'), so existing outsourcing/IT/risk rules apply to coding agents without new regulation.
key_findings.evidence: FINMA expects institutions to 'clearly define the competences and responsibilities for the development, implementation, supervision and use of AI and lay down requirements for model testing, ancillary system controls, documentation standards and training.' For third parties: 'they must determine what data and methods are used... Contractual clauses must govern responsibilities and liability... tests and controls must be put in place.' Survey of ~400 institutions: 50% already use AI; 91% of those use generative AI; data quality, data protection, explainability, and outsourcing rank as the top risks.

key_findings.claim: The recommended org model is a centralized control plane (policy, identity, SIEM, PR-gates, evals, cost controls, vendor-agnostic) with federated execution (per-team agent/tool selection within approved vendors, domain use cases). This is the 'Center of Excellence' pattern adapted for the agentic era — start centralized, federate as confidence grows.
key_findings.evidence: 'Centralize what must be common: policy, platform standards, evals, guardrails, cost controls. Federate what must move fast: business use cases, domain workflows, product ownership.' 'Enterprises typically start centralized, then expand as confidence grows.' Control plane ownership: Central (IT/SecOps); agent selection: Distributed (per-team) within approved vendors — also removes vendor lock-in at the scale phase.

key_findings.claim: The permission/guardrail model for coding agents is least-privilege On-Behalf-Of (OBO) with just-in-time runtime authorization and tool-visibility filtering: the agent inherits only the requesting human's native permissions, policy is checked at every tool call, and tools the user is not entitled to (e.g. merge) never even appear in the agent's context. This is implemented via a policy engine / MCP gateway and repository classification.
key_findings.evidence: 'OBO means the agent executes each action using credentials tied to the requesting user, so the action is limited to that user's native permissions and is attributable in audit logs, with just-in-time authorization executing runtime policy checks at each tool call.' Visibility filtering: 'if a user doesn't have permission to merge code in GitHub, the GitHub merge tool doesn't appear in the agent's context window.' Repo classification: restricted repos (payments, auth, key management, PHI, IaC) are deny-by-default, explicit exception only.

key_findings.claim: ISO/IEC 42001 (AI Management System) is the off-the-shelf operating standard that maps directly to EU AI Act Articles 9-15 (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, human oversight, accuracy) and is becoming a procurement gate. It is the cleanest way for a regulated bank to demonstrate a systematic, auditable AI governance program to FINMA/auditors. KPMG, BSI, Schellman, A-LIGN already certify in Switzerland.
key_findings.evidence: ISO 42001 'demonstrating systematic compliance with Articles 9-15 covering risk management, data governance, technical documentation, human oversight, and accuracy requirements.' EU AI Act human oversight (Art. 14) corresponds to ISO 42001 Annex A.6.2.6. By mid-2026 'Are you ISO 42001 certified or implementing it?' appears in ~40% of enterprise AI vendor RFPs in the EU. Mandatory for certification: 'a centralized registry of every model, its training data sources, and its intended use.'

key_findings.claim: Human oversight should be risk-tiered, not blanket: agents handle verifiable/repetitive work; humans review high-stakes changes. Anthropic's own research shows AI is used in ~60% of work but engineers can 'fully delegate' only 0-20% of tasks — so governance must mandate human review of AI code while routing human attention to what matters (architecture, security, restricted repos), using AI agents to pre-screen the bulk.
key_findings.evidence: Anthropic: 'developers use AI in roughly 60% of their work, they report being able to fully delegate only 0-20% of tasks.' Governance prediction: 'Human oversight shifts from reviewing everything to reviewing what matters' — agentic quality control (AI reviews AI-generated code for security/architecture) becomes standard, while humans handle 'genuinely novel situations, boundary cases, and strategic decisions.' Code review enforcement in the playbook: code-owner review and secret-detection overrides are 'not permitted'; coverage/SAST overrides restricted to named roles with SIEM logging.

key_findings.claim: A dedicated owner and a small standing platform team are governance prerequisites, not optional. Scaled programs name a single accountable owner; the FTE cost of running governance for ~100 devs is modest (~0.6 FTE in Q1, falling to ~0.3 FTE as the discipline matures), but skipping the owner is the top failure mode.
key_findings.evidence: '56% of enterprises that successfully scale AI agent programs name a dedicated owner.' 100-dev case study: rollout absorbed ~0.6 FTE of platform-team attention in Q1, falling to ~0.3 FTE in Q2; executive team funded a 'modest expansion of platform-team capacity to support continuing library and hook governance.' Governance roles: Chief AI Officer (strategy), Agent Owners (tool accountability), Security Champions (risk), Engineering Managers (day-to-day). Skills/agents 'ship with a description, invocation pattern, allow-listed tools, an example trace, and an owner.'

key_findings.claim: The governance maturity gap is the dominant industry reality and the core risk-management argument: most organizations have NO visibility into how AI is used in their SDLC and no enforced governance. This is precisely what triggers regulatory findings and breaches — the gap, not the technology, is the liability.
key_findings.evidence: Deloitte 2026: only 20% of organizations have mature governance models. 81% of organizations 'have no visibility into how AI is actually being used across their development lifecycle.' 68% of organizations lack visibility into AI tools used by developers; only 27% enforce strict governance over AI tool adoption. IBM 2025 Cost of a Data Breach: 63% of breached orgs lacked AI governance policies; shadow AI added ~USD 670,000 to breach costs.

key_findings.claim: Hard contra evidence the CIO must govern against: AI-generated code carries materially higher security defect and rework rates, and ungoverned (shadow) usage is the leading incident vector. These numbers justify mandatory PR gates, SAST/secret scanning, and code provenance labeling rather than blocking adoption.
key_findings.evidence: Veracode 2025: 45% of AI-generated code contains security flaws (Java 70%+ failure rate). Opsera 2026 (250,000+ devs, 60+ orgs): AI-generated code introduces 15-18% more security vulnerabilities than human-written and needs 15-25 pp of rework, offsetting 30-40% productivity gains. Aikido 2026: 1 in 5 breaches caused by AI-generated code. Shadow AI: 57% of employees use AI coding tools without IT approval; unauthorized tools contribute to 1 in 3 security incidents. Fewer than 50% of developers review AI-generated code before committing.

key_findings.claim: A three-layer kill switch and incident runbook (rehearsed quarterly) are required controls — operational resilience is the FINMA-relevant framing (Guidance 05/2025 operational resilience cycle). Governance must be able to instantly revoke an agent at identity, credential, and repository layers.
key_findings.evidence: Three-layer kill switch: (1) Identity layer — suspend user/group at IdP; (2) Credential layer — revoke API keys, OAuth tokens, webhook credentials; (3) Repository layer — lock branch protection, block agent PRs, freeze merges. Incident runbook tabletop: quarterly for first year. Pre-wired kill switch + documented runbook + quarterly rehearsal is one of the seven mandatory controls (SecOps/SRE ownership). FINMA's 2026 supervisory cycle emphasizes operational resilience.

key_findings.claim: EU AI Act exposure for coding agents is mostly indirect but real: ordinary coding assistance is NOT high-risk, but Article 50 transparency (machine-readable marking of AI-generated output) and Annex III classification of the systems being BUILT can apply. The governable action is to label AI-authored PRs and maintain provenance, which the playbook already mandates.
key_findings.evidence: 'AI coding assistants used for standard SDLC tasks almost certainly do not qualify as high-risk AI systems' — but 'the real question is whether the systems built with AI tools... trigger Annex III classification.' Article 50 (active Aug 2, 2026) requires synthetic outputs to be 'marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated.' Playbook control: 'PR labeling required (e.g., agent:claude-code) for traceability to session ID.' High-risk obligations (Articles 8-17, 26, 27, 73) activate August 2, 2026.
